This may result in increased fuel consumption and operational costs, affecting the overall economic viability of non-drop-in fuels. 32 5 SCALING UP BIOFUEL USE: REGIONAL RAIL ENERGY DEMAND, BIOMASS FEEDSTOCK AVAILABILITY, AND ENVIORNMENTAL BENEFITS Argonne’s Bioeconomy AGE and R&D GREET models, and Oak Ridge National Laboratory’s (ORNL’s) BILT model were used to analyze the benefits and tradeoffs associated with the scale up of alternative locomotive fuels and to understand the sufficiency of biomass feedstocks to meet freight rail demand considering competing uses. These models were used to estimate direct and indirect emission reductions, capital funding requirements, construction resource requirements, CAP emissions, water consumption, and energy use with the production and use of these fuels. These results show the amounts of key materials and resources required for scale up by certain points in time (e.g., 2030, 2040, 2050). The U.S. freight rail system was also analyzed to understand specific applications and routes, and to identify promising opportunities for specific alternative fuels. Section 5.1 describes regional resource availability for biofuel production. Section 5.2 characterizes regional freight rail energy use and identifies potential alternative fuel corridors. Section 5.3 describes the scale-up analysis combining biofuel production and demand for the freight rail sector. 5.1 REGIONAL RESOURCE AVAILABILITY FOR BIOFUEL PRODUCTION US DOE 2023 Billion Ton study dataset (DOE, 2024) was used to produce feedstock supply curves and ORNL’s BILT model (Oyedeji et al., 2025) was used to aggregate regional feedstock to conversion facilities. This analysis quantified the economic availability of biomass resources for rail fuels using the Policy Analysis System model (ORNL, 2019) for agricultural residues and energy crops, the Forest Sustainability and Economic Assessment Model (ORNL, 2019) for forestland resources, and waste resource assessments that are ongoing. The comprehensive analysis used the BILT model to quantify spatially explicit allocation of biomass resources to biorefineries for rail applicable biofuels given the TEAs and LCAs from the project. The BILT model, which ORNL developed for the DOE, is an accounting and optimization model that tracks the entire biomass-to-end-use supply chain, including biomass production, transportation, and processing for potential feedstocks, pathways, and end uses. This model solves a series of carbon avoidance costs for specific routes and allows an analysis of routes and end-uses that will result in resource competition. A differentiating feature of BILT is the spatial resolution of inputs and outputs which include the distribution of biomass, infrastructure, and siting of potential facilities for different parts of the biomass, and biofuel/bioproduct conversion process. Details of the decision variables and process of BILT model can be found in (Oyedeji et al., 2025). This model operates by solving a series of mixed-integer programming problems to minimize net carbon emission or total system cost. Based on the LCA/TEA inputs, the model provides results for optimized biorefinery location, movement of feedstock, and total carbon abated. The locations that BILT considers for facility siting are provided via an OR-SAGE framework. OR-SAGE considers several constraints to determine regions of feasibility for siting.
